JSON: Name: plasma_proteome_triage Title: Multivariate plasma proteomic profiling by proximity extension assay to predict undiagnosed cancer in patients presenting with non-specific symptoms Short Hypothesis: A multivariate plasma protein expression signature measured pre-diagnostic by proximity extension assay discriminates patients with undiagnosed cancer from patients with non-cancer diagnoses among individuals presenting with non-specific symptoms, achieving area under the ROC curve >= 0.80 on independent validation. Related Work: Existing pan-cancer diagnostic approaches include single-protein serum biomarkers, multi-analyte cfDNA assays (methylation and fragmentomics), circulating tumor DNA panels, tumor-educated platelet RNA, extracellular vesicle surface profiling, and prior plasma proteomic screens. Single-protein biomarkers provide limited sensitivity and specificity across heterogeneous cancers and are confounded by inflammatory conditions. cfDNA-based methods increase cancer specificity for some solid tumors but show reduced sensitivity for hematologic malignancies and early-stage disease, and often require high sequencing depth and complex bioinformatics. Platelet and extracellular vesicle methods capture tumor signals but face pre-analytic variability and limited clinical validation in symptomatic cohorts. Prior proteomics studies frequently trained on healthy controls or established cancers, producing optimistic performance estimates that do not generalize to diagnostic workflows; many lack independent replication and do not account for inflammatory/autoimmune confounders. Key unresolved issues are robustness to real-world symptomatic populations, discrimination from inflammatory and autoimmune disease, validation across independent clinical sites, and reducing feature panels to clinically feasible assays. Abstract: Objective: To develop and validate a blood-based triage model that uses high-dimensional plasma proteomics measured by proximity extension assay (PEA) to identify undiagnosed cancers among patients presenting with non-specific symptoms. Approach: We propose a multivariate classification pipeline that (1) quantifies ~1,463 plasma proteins by PEA in pre-diagnostic samples, (2) performs stringent QC and between-plate normalization on NPX values, (3) applies univariate filtering and penalized logistic regression for feature selection, and (4) validates performance in an independent clinical cohort. Contribution: The pipeline generates a reproducible protein signature that discriminates cancer from non-cancer diagnoses including autoimmune, inflammatory and infectious conditions, and reports calibration, subgroup performance by diagnosis type and tumor class, and robustness to preprocessing and seed variation. Expected outcome: A validated proteomic triage risk score with reproducible discrimination (target AUC >= 0.80) in symptomatic diagnostic populations, demonstrating feasibility of integrating plasma proteome profiling into clinical triage for prioritizing patients for rapid diagnostic work-up. Experiments: Datasets: Discovery cohort: MEDECA, n=456 patients presenting with non-specific symptoms; EDTA plasma collected at first visit prior to diagnostic work-up; outcome: new cancer diagnosis within 6 months (n≈160) versus non-cancer (n≈296) with annotated subgroups (autoimmune, inflammatory, infectious, no diagnosis). Replication cohort: ALLVOS, n=238 patients, same inclusion criteria; outcome: new cancer diagnosis within 6 months (n≈35) versus non-cancer (n≈203). Protein measurement: Olink Explore PEA, 4 panels, 1,463 proteins; raw counts converted to NPX; QC: remove samples with >50% failed assays; retain proteins measured across panels; apply plate-level median centering (intensity normalization). Baselines: (1) demographic model (age+sex); (2) best single-protein classifier (top individual AUC in discovery); (3) reduced clinical-lab model (standard blood tests available at referral); (4) existing multianalyte cfDNA panel if available for subset (secondary baseline). Model training: Random 70/30 train/test split on discovery cohort; within training set apply three univariate filters: mean NPX difference>1 OR unadjusted t-test p<1e-6 OR univariate AUC>0.7; train penalized logistic regression with L1 (lasso) regularization using 10-fold cross-validation for lambda selection; repeat across 50 random seeds to assess stability. Validation: Evaluate final model on discovery test set and independent replication cohort without retraining. Metrics: primary metric AUC (ROC) with 95% bootstrap CI (2000 bootstraps); secondary metrics sensitivity and specificity at pre-specified thresholds (sensitivity at 90% specificity and specificity at 90% sensitivity), positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV) at cohort prevalence, Brier score, calibration slope/intercept, decision curve analysis (net benefit). Statistical tests: DeLong test for AUC differences versus baselines; McNemar test for paired sensitivity/specificity comparisons. Ablation studies: (A) remove univariate filter criteria one at a time to measure impact on feature set and AUC; (B) iterative panel reduction: evaluate models built using top-N features (N={5,10,20,50}) by importance; (C) subgroup performance: compute AUC stratified by tumor type (hematologic vs solid), stage (localized vs metastatic), and diagnostic subgroup (autoimmune, inflammatory, infectious, no diagnosis); (D) preprocessing sensitivity: compare performance with and without intensity normalization and with alternative normalization seeds. Additional analyses: multicollinearity assessment (variance inflation factors), feature stability across seeds (Jaccard index), and calibration plots. Reproducibility: provide all code and deterministic seeds; report per-protein QC and missingness. Risk Factors and Limitations: Cohort composition bias: discovery and replication cohorts have elevated prevalence of metastatic and hematologic cancers relative to primary care, limiting generalizability to low-prevalence screening populations. Pre-analytical variability: PEA measurements are sensitive to sample handling, storage time, and batch effects; residual batch effects may confound signatures. Confounding by inflammation: many candidate proteins are acute-phase or inflammation-associated, reducing specificity against autoimmune and inflammatory diseases and producing false positives. Limited subgroup power: small sample sizes in replication cancer cases and in disease subgroups will yield wide confidence intervals and limit reliable estimates for tumor-type and stage-specific performance. Feature overfitting: high-dimensional input vs moderate sample size risks model overfitting despite penalization; selected proteins may not replicate in external platforms or absolute-quantification assays. Detection bias: PEA platform favors soluble/circulating proteins and under-represents membrane-anchored or intracellular tumor markers. Clinical impact limitations: positive results may increase downstream imaging and invasive procedures with potential harms and resource use; model PPV will decrease in lower-prevalence settings. Data access and privacy: patient-level clinical data cannot be openly shared without agreements, which may hinder external validation. Regulatory and assay scalability: translating a large multi-protein panel to a clinically deployable, cost-effective assay requires platform standardization and analytical validation that are non-trivial.
